## Summary There is a medium severity vulnerability in Traefik's Kubernetes Ingress provider that allows an actor with permission to create or update `Ingress` or `Service` resources in one namespace to reference `Middleware`, `ServersTransport`, and `TLSOption` resources from other namespaces through annotations. Unlike the Kubernetes CRD provider, which rejects such references when `allowCrossNamespace` is disabled, the annotation path performs no namespace validation, partially bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation. In multi-tenant clusters, this can expose another tenant's secrets, such as credentials injected by a `Headers` middleware or a client certificate configured in a `ServersTransport`. The fix introduces the `crossProviderNamespaces` option on the Kubernetes providers, which must be explicitly set to restrict which namespaces are allowed to use cross-provider references; when it is left unset, all namespaces remain allowed. ## Patches - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v2.11.46 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.6.17 - https://github.com/traefik/traefik/releases/tag/v3.7.1 ## For more information If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, please [open an issue](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/issues).

[PoC router.middlewares intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-authtxt) - [Test Setup](#test-setup) ## Description When using the Ingress and Service Annotations, it is possible to reference Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions from foreign namespaces. While this is disallowed by default for Traefik's Kubernetes CRDs (by the [Configuration Option ``providers.kubernetesCRD.allowCrossNamespace``](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/install-configuration/providers/kubernetes/kubernetes-crd/#opt-providers-kubernetesCRD-allowCrossNamespace)), no validation is done when using Annotations on K8s Ingress and Service resources. An attacker can include these resources in an Ingress or Service configuration and thereby partially bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation. In certain cases, this will give an attacker access to data of services in other namespaces, for instance: - If a middleware adds an API access token through the Header middleware, an attacker can steal this token. - An attacker could include a ServersTransport that does client certificate authentication against a service to access this service. - An attacker could include a ForwardAuth middleware to gain access to the internal response headers of the forward auth service and thus might steal internal tokens. ## Affected Version The vulnerability was tested in the current Traefik version v3.6.5. Older versions are affected, too. ## Source Code References Ingress and Service Annotations are vulnerable. There is no check implemented in: [``pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress/kubernetes.go``](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/blob/f794f8a29491b8467868811a3142a48e8f0a3854/pkg/provider/kubernetes/ingress/kubernetes.go#L202) Traefik's Kubernetes CRDs are not vulnerable and prevent cross namespace access: [``pkg/provider/kubernetes/crd/kubernetes_http.go``](https://github.com/traefik/traefik/blob/f794f8a29491b8467868811a3142a48e8f0a3854/pkg/provider/kubernetes/crd/kubernetes_http.go#L170) ## Prerequisites - Traefik is installed in Kubernetes - No special configuration is required as the ``kubernetesIngress`` provider is enabled by default - The attacker needs permission to create or modify Ingress or Service resources in one namespace - The name of the namespace and the name of the Middleware, TLSOption, or ServersTransport resource they want to target ## Impact An attacker can include Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions resources from foreign namespaces in their own Ingress or Service configuration, thereby partially bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation. In certain cases, this will give an attacker access to data of services in other namespaces. ## Security Researcher / Reporter - Lorin Lehawany of ERNW Enno Rey Netzwerke GmbH - Sven Nobis of ERNW Enno Rey Netzwerke GmbH ## Proof of Concept The following descriptions explain the exploitation in detail for the two affected resource types Middleware and ServersTransport. The proof of concept (PoC) was tested in a Traefik setup installed via Helm chart in version `37.4.0`, but with the most recent Traefik app version ``v3.6.5`` and the default configuration. See the [test setup section](#test-setup) for details. ### Middleware Proof Of Concept The following steps demonstrate the problem with the affected ``router.middlewares`` annotation. This PoC even works with restrictive Network Policies set. #### Step 1: Preparation First, the namespaces `traefik-victim` and `traefik-attacker` are created: ```sh kubectl create namespace traefik-victim kubectl create namespace traefik-attacker namespace/traefik-victim created namespace/traefik-attacker created ``` In the next steps, the resources in the `victim.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-victim`, and the resources in the `attacker.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-attacker`. #### Step 2: Create Victim's Resources This step creates some resources to simulate a typical vulnerable setup with an application that uses Traefik and Ingress. The [`victim.yaml`](#poc-routermiddlewares--victimyaml) creates an Ingress resource with the name `traefik-ingress` in the namespace `traefik-victim`. The Ingress exposes the victim's application under the hostname `traefik-victim.gke.gcp.ernw.eu` and routes all requests with the path prefix `/example-app` to an internal service on port 80. The victim's application is exposed via the service `example-app-service` and protects its resources with an API token internally. The application itself is a simple nginx, which is configured using the ConfigMap to deliver a static HTML page. The server rejects any request that does not contain the predefined `X-API-Token` HTTP header with the correct value. This simulates an internal application that relies on a secret API token for authorization and assumes that only trusted users can provide this token. Further, two Traefik middlewares are defined: `basicauth` and `addheader`. `basicauth` middleware enforces HTTP Basic Authentication, and the `addheader` adds an `X-API-Token` request header with a secret value to all incoming requests to allow access for authorized users. This setup is deployed by the following commands: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f victim.yaml -n traefik-victim ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created service/example-app-service created deployment.apps/example-app created middleware.traefik.io/addheader created middleware.traefik.io/basicauth created secret/authsecret created configmap/nginx-conf created ``` The screenshot `victim-example-app.png` below shows the basic authentication, which is required for users to access the protected resources. After successful authentication, the user is logged in, and the static HTML content is displayed, as shown in the second screenshot (`victim-app.png`) below. The file shows [intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-wo-authtxt) and [intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-auth.txt](#poc-routermiddlewares-intern-demo-access-victims-pod-with-authtxt) show that authentication is required when accessing the service internally. #### Step 3: Create Attacker Resources The [`attacker.yaml`](#poc-routermiddlewares--attackeryaml) contains the resources to steal the token from the ``addheader`` Middleware. This attacker-controlled Ingress is deployed in the attacker's namespace and configured to use the victim's Traefik middleware through [the ``router.middlewares`` annotation](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/routing-configuration/kubernetes/ingress/#on-ingress). The attacker-controlled deployment uses a simple ``whoami`` container which reflects all HTTP response headers. This is used to steal the victim's credentials. This setup is deployed by the following commands in the namespace `traefik-attacker`: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f attacker.yaml -n traefik-attacker ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created deployment.apps/whoami created service/whoami created ``` The following excerpt from the Traefik Pod shows that the resource from the victim's namespace is configured in the attacker's namespace: for the victim’s internal application, without being authorized to the victim’s service. This is done via an attacker accessing his exposed service, which reflects all HTTP response headers, including the `X-Api-Token: example-secret-api-token`. The screenshot ``attacker-controlled-pod-whoami-reflects-all-http-response-headers.png`` below shows this. ### ServersTransport Proof Of Concept The following steps demonstrate the problem with the affected ServersTransport annotation. This PoC does not work if Network Policies filter traffic to the victim's services from the attacker's namespace. #### Step 1: Create Victim and Attacker Namespaces First, the namespaces `traefik-victim` and `traefik-attacker` are created: ```sh kubectl create namespace traefik-victim kubectl create namespace traefik-attacker namespace/traefik-victim created namespace/traefik-attacker created ``` In the next steps, the resources in the `victim.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-victim`, and the resources in the `attacker.yaml` are created in the namespace `traefik-attacker`. #### Step 2: Create Victim Resources This step creates some resources to simulate a typical vulnerable setup with an application which is using Traefik and Ingress. It simulates a setup where the internal service (`mtls-nginx`) is protected with mTLS. The [`victim.yaml`](#poc-serviceserverstransport--victimyaml) creates multiple resources to demonstrate the following scenario: A user accesses the application via HTTPS, where access from the outside is restricted through basic authentication and client certificate authentication is enforced inside the cluster. The resource `traefik-ingress` exposes the victim's application under the hostname `traefik-victim.gke.gcp.test.eu` with the path prefix `/example-app` and enforces basic authentication via the `basicauth` middleware. The Ingress forwards traffic to the Service `mtls-nginx`, which represents the nginx Pod. The `mtls-nginx` Service routes traffic to the deployment `mtls-nginx`, which runs the nginx web server. For demonstration-purposes the web server delivers some static content. The ServersTransport resource with the name `serverstransport` defines the mTLS settings for Traefik. It requires to specify the server name, root CA, and client certificate to authenticate with the nginx. To simulate a more realistic scenario, the defined Middleware `basicauth` enforces basic authentication using the Secret `authsecret` for username/password so that access from the outside is restricted. This setup is deployed by the following commands: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f vicitim.yaml -n traefik-victim ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created service/mtls-nginx created deployment.apps/mtls-nginx created serverstransport.traefik.io/serverstransport created configmap/nginx-mtls-conf created configmap/client-ca-cert created secret/nginx-tls created secret/client-cert-secret created secret/nginx-cert created middleware.traefik.io/basicauth created secret/authsecret created ``` #### Step 3: Create Attacker Resources The [`attacker.yaml`](#poc-serviceserverstransport--attackeryaml) contains the resources to get access the victim's mTLS protected service. The attacker's setup exposes the host `traefik-attacker.gke.gcp.ernw.eu` that forwards traffic to a `socat` proxy, which routes HTTPS connections directly to the victim’s mTLS service to authenticate successfully. Traefik perform client certificate authentication with the victim's client certificate through the configuration of the [``service.serverstransport`` annotation](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/routing-configuration/kubernetes/ingress/#on-service). The attacker does not need RBAC access to the victim's namespace to do it. An attacker can use the ``service.serverstransport`` annotation to do mTLS authentication against other services inside and outside of the cluster, too. This setup is deploy by the following commands in the namespace `traefik-attacker`: ```sh $ kubectl apply -f attacker.yaml -n traefik-attacker ingress.networking.k8s.io/traefik-ingress created service/socat-proxy created deployment.apps/socat-proxy created ``` The following excerpt from the Traefik Pod shows that the resource from the victim's namespace is configured in the attacker's Client Certificate to authenticate against protected resource living in the victim's own namespace As a result, the attacker is able to authenticate with the client certificate from the victim's namespace against the victim's service and thus bypass the mTLS authentication. The screenshot ``attacker-accessing-victims-protected-resources.png`` below shows this. ## Recommendation Disallow cross-namespaces access for annotations-based configuration by default, as in Traefik's Kubernetes CRDs, and offer a [Configuration Option like ``providers.kubernetesCRD.allowCrossNamespace``](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/install-configuration/providers/kubernetes/kubernetes-crd/#opt-providers-kubernetesCRD-allowCrossNamespace) to allow it. ## Appendix ### Resources #### PoC router.middlewares / victim.yaml ```yaml kind: Ingress apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 metadata: name: traefik-ingress namespace: traefik-victim annotations: traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.entrypoints: web,websecure traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.middlewares: "traefik-victim-basicauth@kubernetescrd,traefik-victim-addheader@kubernetescrd" spec: ingressClassName: traefik rules: -
